title_short: Ernie Richmann III · Why Safety Town Matters
headline: He taught in Painesville schools for 35 years and had three students killed by trains; he made the little train the children now practise on at Safety Town.
story: Ernie Richmann III is a 40-year Lion and taught in Painesville City Schools for 35 years. Three of his students were hit and killed by trains. Another student in the school system was hit by a car. This program is important to him.

The turn: the viewer expects a grief story. Instead, the man who lost students to trains is the man who made the little train the children practise on. Put the train on screen while he says it. Then Gena says what the program is, and his son Ernie IV closes it: the kids won't forget this.

Loops: L1 “Who is this man, and whose students were they?” opens at 0:00 and closes at about 0:10 (35 years in Painesville schools). L2 “What does this have to do with a bright little pretend town?” opens at 0:00 and closes in the button. Stakes: children here were killed on the tracks; one free week in a pretend town, run by volunteers, teaches the next ones.
do: Open on Ernie's face with <q>THREE OF HIS STUDENTS DIED</q> already on screen on frame 1. It does not animate on.
Hold about 1 s of quiet after the first line before anything moves.
Name super at 00:06, lower left, 2 s: Ernie Richmann III / taught in Painesville 35 years. Spelling Richmann.
Put the little train (5V0A8847.MP4) on screen on “The little train, I made that.”
The last picture before the end card is children, not an adult.
dont: Do not say or show a child's name, age or date. We do not have them.
Do not say the child hit by the car died, and do not say Safety Town was founded because of these deaths. He says neither.
No how-he-joined, who-recruited-him or friends-he-made lines. Never “Richmond” on screen.
No whooshes, zoom punches or sad piano under the deaths.
No Lions logo or AYH lockup before the end card, including the Welcome sign and the banner shots in the B-roll.

Painesville Children's Safety Town, 10 June 2026. Lav audio WAVs; times are mm:ss.s in each WAV from the shoot's caption file (SRT line times). The transcript spells the family Richmond/Richman/Jenna: the names are Ernie Richmann III, Ernie Richmann IV and Gena Richmann. Some off-topic lines are left out.
--- DJI_02_20260609_235016.WAV — Ernie Richmann III
[00:18.3] [Interviewer] So, we'll start just with you stating your name and your role within the Lions Club.
[00:25.6] [name only: spelled Richmann, not a bite] Okay. Well, I'm Ernie Richmond. I'm a 40-year member, and I'm currently a membership chair and secretary,
[00:34.2] and then I have a couple positions in the district. I'm a zone chair, I'm diabetes chair for the district,
[00:43.2] and I'm diabetes chair for the state of Ohio for all the Lions Clubs.
[00:51.6] I've served as president, treasurer, everything.
[00:59.9] [Interviewer] Well, first question is this. Are you happy?
[01:03.7] I'm a very happy person. I have a very supportive family, and I think it's great what Lions Clubs are doing.
[01:16.5] [Interviewer] Tell me about how you first found out about Lions Club.
[01:21.9] [do not use: how he joined] Okay. Well, a gentleman that I highly respected just asked me.
[01:27.1] [do not use: how he joined] I didn't really know what I was getting into and kind of found out about things as I was in it a few years.
[01:34.9] [do not use: how he joined] He lived to be 103, and he was even going to meetings when he was 100.
[01:41.9] [do not use: how he joined] His wife lived to be 99, and I stopped letting him drive me to the Lions Club meeting when I found out he was
[01:50.8] [do not use: how he joined] going blind.
[01:54.9] [do not use: how he joined] Yeah, I had no idea really about it. I didn't really know anything about Lions. I just signed up anyway.
[02:02.9] [Interviewer] What was that like, those early years like for you, being a new member, meeting new people, growing in relationship,
[02:11.9] [Interviewer] and getting a better idea of what the organization does? What was that like for you?
[02:15.9] I went to all the meetings, and I went to all the service projects and things,
[02:21.9] but it's quite different today because our club is way more active currently than it was in those early days.
[02:30.9] We had a rose sale every year. We rang the bells for Salvation Army at Christmas time.
[02:39.3] We did a few other things. We had some other fundraisers, maybe a raffle ticket or something,
[02:45.3] but we're doing something every single month, and I'm really glad about all of that.
[02:57.5] [Interviewer] Tell me about how it was for you to grow in relationship, grow in commitment, to the point that now,
[03:05.5] [Interviewer] and you probably know this about yourself, but you've connected quite a few members here to the club.
[03:11.5] [Interviewer] You're that connecting point that a lot of people mentioned.
[03:14.5] [do not use: how he joined] I have sponsored quite a few people. Some of them are no longer with the club, but many are.
[03:21.5] [do not use: how he joined] My wife finally joined. Ernie joined. Jenna, his wife, joined. His mother-in-law joined.
[03:30.1] [do not use: how he joined] My neighbor across the street joined, and a number of other people, too.
[03:36.5] [do not use: how he joined] Oh, Rick Webb, who you interviewed. I sponsored Rick.
[03:40.5] [do not use: how he joined] We were running buddies. We were both in the running club, and I don't run anymore.
[03:48.5] I'm still pretty active physically. In fact, last weekend, I walked 50 miles in an ultra marathon in Canal Fulton.
[04:00.5] I've still got good energy. It was more than 17 hours. I just walked the whole thing.
[04:10.5] I had runners. I'm fairly fit. I have type 1 diabetes, and that's kind of how I got to be diabetes, too.
[04:23.5] That wasn't required for that position, but I give diabetes presentations.
[04:31.1] I helped a lot with all these safety town buildings because I'm also pretty handy.
[04:39.6] There was a lot of other members that helped with that. The little train, I made that.
[04:51.4] [Interviewer] How do you see the Lions Club becoming more than just a club of members and more like a family?
[04:58.0] [Interviewer] How was that for you? Was there any key moment where you felt like, these are my people, this is where I belong?
[05:05.0] One thing, we've had some work days out of Camp Homi, Dakota.
[05:10.5] That's a camp for diabetic children not too far from here in Newbury, Ohio.
[05:15.5] We've had, not just from our club, but a lot of local clubs have gone on those work days.
[05:49.8] I'm there from time to time. They'll have two more tour days coming up soon.
[05:59.8] We haven't determined the dates yet. That was one thing I did really grab onto.
[06:08.1] One kid at the camp said that this was the only time they really felt normal.
[06:15.1] That was enough for me. I kind of key in on that.
[06:22.1] [Interviewer] For clubs like the Lions Club and really any other kind of commitment people want to make, it's difficult.
[06:33.8] [Interviewer] Specifically, it seems to be most difficult for the age groups of 30s, 40s, 50s.
[06:40.8] [Interviewer] When you're kind of peak career, probably kids in home that you're trying to manage.
[06:46.8] [Interviewer] Life is busy. But even for anyone not specifically in those age ranges and those stages of life, life is busy.
[06:54.8] [Interviewer] What's your encouragement for other people? How did you find the time to be so involved in the Lions Club?
[07:04.4] I was teaching. I really didn't know how much time it would take. I just joined anyway.
[07:12.1] When I talk to somebody about the Lions Club, I tell them we don't require a new member to attend every single meeting.

[07:34.1] You don't have to be at every single function. Just help when you can.
[07:43.3] If you're more concerned about your career, you have young children, all of that.
[07:50.8] Even some of the older people, they have a lot of activities with their grandchildren.
[07:58.8] Now they have more time to travel. Help out when you can. I don't have any problem with that.
[08:04.8] I think in the old days, it was more of a requirement to attend everything.
[08:12.0] This is not true with our club. We don't do it that way.
[08:16.8] Did that answer the question?
[08:19.2] [Interviewer] Yeah, that was good. Tell me about you personally. What is great about being a Lion?
[08:29.5] I just think there's a whole lot more besides my own little world.
[08:34.4] There's a lot of needs in our country and globally. Maybe I could just help just a little bit.
[08:44.3] Do what I can do. I taught in Painesville City Schools for 35 years.
[08:53.1] I had three students that got hit and killed by trains. We have train safety here.
[09:00.0] I didn't have this student, but there was another student in this school system that was hit by a car in the middle of
[09:07.8] the street.
[09:10.5] This program is important.
[09:15.9] [Interviewer] What excites you about the future of Lion's Club?
[09:19.2] We are getting more and more younger people.
[09:23.0] That Cubs program that we have is involving younger people with children.
[09:31.0] We're a very diverse club. We don't care what somebody's skin color is or their religion or even their politics.
[09:47.0] What binds us together is we just want to serve the community.
[09:52.0] If somebody wants to do that, you're good for this club.
[10:29.4] I don't think so.
[10:32.1] I think our strength is we're welcoming to most folks, any age, men and women, just people that want to serve.
[10:45.6] We're flexible. I think I said all of that.
